Adjudication. Two reviewers have already judged these 12 cases and gave different answers. Their answers and reasons are shown below each conversation as Review X and Review Y, without names and in no fixed order. Read the conversation first and make your own judgment; you may agree with either review or with neither.

In this study, we examine whether people understand a conversation in ways that could affect what they do next. You will review 12 short cases involving map directions or a social deduction game. Each case identifies two people and provides the conversation and relevant task information up to a marked stopping point.

Read the material and decide whether those two people’s understanding would lead to the same task outcome, different task outcomes, or whether you need more information to tell. For example, choosing different landmarks could lead to different routes. Different wording can still lead to the same outcome.

Base your judgment on the material shown up to the stopping point. A reply such as “Okay” may leave someone’s understanding unclear. In the game cases, consider how the players interpret the same statement or event. Different claims or accusations can also reflect disagreement or deception. Choose “Not enough information” when the conversation does not establish the comparison.
